items.speaker: Leader of the House
items.text: I move, That pursuant to section 131(a) of the Electoral Act
1993, a vacancy in the Northland Electoral Dist rict having arisen in  the period of six
months prior to the date of th e expiration of this Parliament, no writ be issued for the
election of a member of Parliament for that Electoral District to supply the vacancy
occasioned by the resignation of John McGregor Carter.
The Hon John Carter resigned his parlia mentary seat on 17 July 2011, creating a
vacancy in his Northland electorate seat. Section 131 of the Electoral Act 1993 provides
that no writ shall be issued for a by-election if a general election is to be held within 6
months of the occurrence of the vacancy, and a resolution is passed by a majority of 75
percent of all the members of the House of Representatives to  the effect that a writ is
not to be issued to supply the vacancy.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: The Labour Party is
supporting this motion. In fact, if we were not, the motion would not have been moved
and certainly would not be e ffective if it passed, vis-à-vis section 131 of the Electoral
Act. I think it is appropriate. It is an unusua l situation to be in, to follow a member’s
4 Aug 2011 Member Vacancy 20367
valedictory, but I think “Hone” Carter had one of those vale dictories of the type where
many members of the House would have pref erred him to go on a bit longer. It was
entertaining. It was probably like the memb er—always entertaining, always caring, and
someone who was one of the characters of th e House. I tend to say, and it might be a
sign of my own ageing, that they seem to be fewer and farther between, the people who
were elected as a result of their good organisation in an el ectorate, tying up the seat to
get the National Party nomination, and then c ontinuing to keep it tied up in a way that
meant that over a period of time—notwithst anding a number of perceived, and actual,
sins—Mr Carter was able to be totally unchallenged as to his right to represent an area
that he built as a National Party stronghold, and one that was not always the safest of
National seats. If we look at the demographi cs of the seat it should not necessarily be
so, but, as a result of his character and his work, it became a safe National seat.
I was lucky enough to travel wi th Mr Carter, I think at the beginning of 1994, to the
United States. At that stage the then two-thirds owners of Telecom—two US
companies—hosted us. I think these days one could not think of many less likely
members of Parliament to be the ones seen to be leading the Parl iament in technology
matters, but the objective was for some members of Parliament to gain a working
understanding of technology. I think it is fair to say that I understood from that time
about convergence, and it is in teresting to see that what was predicted to John Carter
and me is beginning to happen now, which is probably close to 15 years after the
expectation of when it would occur.
We had some interesting conversations. Pr obably my most inte resting conversation
with John Carter related to when I had heard him, late one day, talking to John Banks on
the radio.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Ha, ha!

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I make it clear it was not the time when he was found
to be offending; it was an earlier occasion. Su bsequent to that, we had a discussion, I
think at the diplomats and pa rliamentarians cricket match, when we were both fit and
able enough to play. I indicated  to him that I had heard him, I had recognised his voice,
and I thought that it was unwise for him to have done such a thing. Well, he is a bit like
me: slightly stubborn and does not always learn from the first mistake, unless he is told
off. There was a repeat performance, the fall-out from which was his fall from grace and
resignation as a whip. Probably, more important , I think it led to the interruption, for a
period of 15 years, of the career of John Banks, who was not  reappointed as a Minister
after that, and suffered the even worse fate of not being allowed to travel to South
Africa to the Parliamentary Rugby World Cup in 1995. The Rt Hon Jim Bolger—now,
of course, Sir James Bolger—forbade him from going, thinking that what were clearly
racist comments would not go down well in the new South Africa. I think it is fair to say
that it could have caused—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Carter?

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: No, Banks’ comments; Banks’ comments were
actually worse than Carter’s comments, beca use there was a suggestion that the thing
had been jacked up, and Banks at the time wa s a Minister and therefore the offence was
more serious. As I say, Carter had been warned and he obviously was caught out later
on.
But having said that, one of the important points about John Carter, and the thing that
I valued the most, was that he always kept  his word. We had a nu mber of arrangements
that were made behind the Chair, over a period of tim e, and John made it clear, when he
had made an agreement, when he had indicated that he would have “best endeavours” to
deliver, he certainly tried very hard, and he was always very thorough in that when there
was a problem with what he was endeavourin g to do, he would come back, he would
20368 Member Vacancy 4 Aug 2011
indicate and there was clarity in the situ ation. I think that was a good sign of his
integrity.
I think John Carter has a good job in going to  Rarotonga. I think there is a bit of a
practice—though not normally for electorate MPs, and I will refer to that soon—of
members of Parliament taking up diplomatic  postings. Of course, he follows in the
footsteps of the late Brian Donnelly in bei ng the member of Parliament appointed to go
to Avarua. I think it is fair to say that a number of us, on occasion, have indicated that
such an approach would not be the worst pos sible thing. I had five words that I think I
said to Helen Clark two or three times while she was Prime Minister when I was in her
bad books, and they were “Port Vila, Hanoi, New York.” For some reason she did not
value my diplomatic skills in quite the wa y that would lead her to think it might be
better for me to be appointed a diplomat, ra ther than continuing my endeavours in the
House.

items.speaker: Louise Upston
items.text: I wonder why, Trevor. I wonder why.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Well, I have always resp ected her judgment. Under
MMP, I signal—not now, and probably not even as part of the next review, but at some
stage—that it would be worth looking at having a system whereby we do not have to go
to a by-election when we have this sort of arrangement, even if it is prior to the 6-month
period before an election. A number of matu re democracies are able, when they have
this sort of system, to have people who are effectively deputy electorate members—
people who, when a member of Parliament b ecomes a Minister, step in and effectively
become an electorate member or effectively become a list member. There is a reversal
of roles, which means that the Minister  is freed up from doing the work in the
electorate. It is taken over by someone else, but with the proviso—I think in all cases—
that that reversal can be worked backwards again.
I wonder whether at some stage we need to look at the possibility of another member
stepping into the electorate seat role. I th ink, because we do not generally affect the
proportionality of Parliament—we are much  more party-based—that it is something
worth looking at. But I think we are having a little bit of trouble at the moment getting
universal acceptance of the role of the list MP and the way that things work, and we
might not be quite at the point where we co uld convince the public that that sort of
system should be developed. I th ink that would raise the possi bility of another list MP
coming to Parliament, replacing the pe rson who transfers over, keeping the
proportionality in Parliament, and thereby saving millions of dollars in some cases in
by-elections. I actually quite enjoy by-elections , but all of us know they will not make
any difference to the eventual decisions that go through this House.
Labour supports this motion, and we wish J ohn Carter well, but I hope that at some
future stage we do not have to pass similar motions.

items.speaker: Hon RICK BARKER
items.text: This is an unusual event. Normally it is impossible
to say things about a member of Parliament  who has resigned their position. Normally
the valedictory is said and that is it, but I have been given the rare  opportunity to talk
about—I have just learnt his full name—John McGregor Carter.
I have known John for quite some time and would like to make a few comments
about him, but before I do so I make the ob servation that this circumstance we are in
here is very unusual. I have been here  since 1993, and I can recall this situation
happening only once before, and that was with the resignation of Michael Laws in the
Hawke’s Bay seat. Michael Laws got himself in to a spot of bother about a signature on
a so-called referendum or survey done in his area, and he thought the only honourable
thing for him to do was to resign. At that point there was no election date set. Within a
m
atter of hours the then Prime Minister, the Rt Hon Jim Bolger, announced the election
day. As a consequence of that, the House coul d consider a motion to say that there was
no need to have a by-election because it was within 6 months of an election.
4 Aug 2011 Member Vacancy 20369
It was a remarkable circumstance to have an election date set so early, and it changed
what happened in this Hous e. I was going to undertake some work with the then
Minister of Justice, Mr Graham, but when I approached him after the adjournment of
the House he said he could not do that work then because we were in an election
campaign. The whole thing changed.
We are in a remarkable situation now, because we have an election date set so far out
but still the House carries on its work. It has not quite got to the election phase yet.
I have worked with John over a long period of time. I put on th e record that I found
John to be a very good member of Parliament and an honourable member of Parliament.
I dealt with John on many occasions as a whip. Those people who have held the
position of a whip in this House will realise that there is quite a distinct and different
relationship between the whips. One of the roles of the Opposition whip, which was a
position I held, was to make the life of the senior Government whip as difficult as
possible, and I did the best I could. I pl agued him with all so rts of tricks—moving
people around, moving motions, and so on—but al l through this John kept his sense of
humour. John was always very level-headed and simply accepted that this was the way
the role was played.
John was always very good to deal with. In my opinion he was a man of integrity.
Whenever I had an agreement with John there was never any doubt about the agreement
being held to. His word was his bond, and I think this is a fine quality in him for New
Zealand when he takes up his position repr esenting New Zealand overseas. I think the
people he represents will find him, as I did, to be very tr ustworthy and very reliable. I
have a great deal of respect for the man.
That brings me to the point that we now find that the far north has no representative.
That is effectively what has happened. It is  unrepresented. Some people could exercise
some concern about this, but I am not sure th at all would be of that opinion. This is no
disrespect to John personally.
I recount one occasion when that fine institution of this Parliament, the Parliamentary
Rugby Team, was invited by John Carter to tour the far north and play some games. We
were playing in Kait āia, and the local team was a team of locals who were very large,
strong-looking, farm-type men. Two of them had seen some service in the All Blacks,
and they looked a pretty formidable crew, I can tell members that. At one part of the
game the ball was kicked up high into the air, and the line of defence for the
Parliamentary Rugby Team was John McGregor Carter. A line of forwards was fanned
out—a large line of forwards—and they were hunting as a pack. They had one target,
and it was the local member of Parliament. The captain of the Parliamentary Rugby
Team shouted so all could hear “Don’t kick ! Don’t kick! For God’s sake, don’t kick!”,
but John was torn between two lines: self-p reservation and orders. John chose self-
preservation. He put hi s boot into the ball, it slid off th e side of his boot and spiralled
away, and this line of four lumpy forwards  scooped up the ball, powered over the line,
and scored a try. The captain was standing there shaking his head, and then someone
from the sideline said “Don’t worry. He doesn’t listen to us either.” There was good
humour. I want to say that even though it is politics, people can see the humour in it,
and I am sure they said that with affection.
One thing I will miss from John is his jokes. I do not think I can recount any of them
here tonight—partly because it is a family show and partly because I cannot remember
them all. Whenever there was a down moment in the House, John would give me a
nudge and say something. I would meet him out the back and he would recount his
latest list of yarns.
He was also a person with incredible know ledge of how this place operates. I am
sure that in recent times National will have  found that John’s advice on tactics and how
20370 Member Vacancy 4 Aug 2011
to operate things in the Hous e has been invaluable. I can th ink of no other position than
when we were discussing the Auckland bill. Once John moved back into the centre
stage we thought we have a tough opponent here, and so it proved to be.
I am sure National will miss John, just as Labour will. We do not  always have to
agree with people in this House; I do not thi nk that is important. What we have to see,
though, is that they make a contribu tion, and, without a doubt, John made a
contribution. It was not always in the debate s, but he certainly made a contribution in
how the House was structured, how the H ouse was organised, and how it ran. He was
very conscious of the principles of this H ouse, its protocol, and its traditions. He was
always very supportive of those and made sure  that people underst ood that these were
the rules of how the place ran. Yes, there are formal rules and the Standing Orders. Yes,
there are Speakers’ rulings. But there are other ways in which people go about their
business with integrity and by viewing with  due respect each member here as an
honourable member, and John was certainly on e who upheld that. From that point of
view I will miss him, because that collectiv e knowledge is important to how this place
runs.
I thought John made a great contribution. Ye s, he might have cluttered up the car-
park down below with his collection of ancient and semi-ancient vehicles—

items.speaker: Chris Tremain
items.text: There are plenty of parks down there.

items.speaker: Hon RICK BARKER
items.text: There are plenty of parks now; the parking space has
increased. The humour will be gone, just as I miss Mike Moore’s humour around the
place. When I talk about Mike Moore and John Carter I think how Mike Moore always
used to say when someone was saying good th ings about him: “Oops, I must be dead;
they’re praising me.” I want to say to John th at we are not saying th is because we think
that about him. We have always thought this.
Finally, I want to turn to the last point, which is the issue raised by the Hon Trevor
Mallard—that we now have a vaca ncy in John Carter’s seat and we still have in this
House 121 members of Parliament. I do think th ere is a gap here, a nd I think we should
put our collective minds to how this could be better managed in the future. It could be
that the public find it acceptable to have a vacancy for 6 months. I am sure the public in
the far north are thankful that we are going to pass this resolution, because the last thing
they will want, I am sure, is two electi ons in 6 months—two occasions when their
letterboxes are festooned with newsletters a nd direct leafleting, there are ads in the
paper, hoardings up all around the place, and adverts for votes, driving the public mad. I
think their tolerance is for an election once every 3 years; any sooner than that becomes
a little less tolerable. So I think the far north public will see this motion as a good thing.
On the downside there is no clearly recognised person to whom they can go as their
local representative. Yes, there are list MPs in the area, and, yes, we could look at
formalising those things in the future. Th e Hon Trevor Mallard has made a very good
suggestion. I also accept the point he has ma de that, given that we are looking at our
electoral system, this is most probably not the best time to look at such a detail. But it is
something we should keep in the back of our minds and think of.
In closing, I would just like to say a fina l thankyou to John for all the contributions
he has made here over the years. I want to say thank you to John for all the goodwill he
has shown to me, and I want to say thank you to John for the way in which he has
conducted his work in this House. I persona lly found him to be a man of integrity,
someone I could do deals with, and someone whose word was his bond. I think that is a
very important thing. I never had to ask John for an email or a letter to confirm
something. I knew that if John stood there, l ooked me in the eye, and said what would
happen, I could go to the bank and say it w ould happen. There are not many people one
can say that about. I would lik e to say it about more people, but I can certainly say it
4 Aug 2011 Member Vacancy 20371
about John Carter. I do not think there are ma ny finer tributes one could say to a person
than that he always kept his word. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: I must say that it was a pleasure
listening to the members of the Labour  Opposition being so gracious about my
colleague the Hon John Carter. It was great to hear the en thusiasm of the Hon Clayton
Cosgrove when he heard that I was about to speak on the good news in terms of Vote
Health, because, indeed, it is very good news. This year $528 million has been made
available; $1.5 billion has been made available since National came into power in 2008.
But I want to talk about health promotion and disease prevention, which is something
that Labour goes on and on and on about. We have an absolutely incredible record. First
of all, I will mention immunisation. Back in 2007 in the order of 76 percent of 2-year-
olds were covered. Now that figure has rocketed  up to 90 percent. That is an absolutely
excellent achievement in the last few years.

items.speaker: Let us look at the second thing
items.text: home  insulation. Under the Labour Government
something like 2,000 or 3,000 homes were insu lated. Under the National Government
100,000 homes have been insulated, which is another great public health achievement.
There is no doubt that a whole spectrum of re spiratory illnesses is being prevented by
this initiative, which has been executed so ably by the National Government.
Let us go on to rheumatic fever. This Budget puts $12 million into clinics for
children. I think the plan is that something like 22,000 children will be covered in this
particular initiative, which was something th at the Labour Government talked about as
one of its many, many priorities  and strategies year after year. But what did National
do? We put it into action.
20372 Estimates Debate 4 Aug 2011
Then we go on to smoking. What happened under Labour? There was something like
a 10 percent increase in excise tax in 9 years. National has executed a 30 percent
increase in excise tax, and we know that this  is one of the most effective methods in
reducing smoking and all the ill health that is associated with it.
Let us look at the ro ll-out of before-school checks . There were something like 1,000
or so under the Labour Government. All Labour could do was about 1,000 checks.
Under National 100,000 children have had before-school checks, and something in the
order of 8,500 children have gone on to have th eir eyesight corrected or have various

There is also the area of maternity. I must say that if ever there was an area of health
promotion and disease prevention, it must be the area of maternity.

items.speaker: CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: It is great to be able  to take a call in the
estimates debate on Vote Health. I want to focus on some of the achievements the
Minister of Health, Tony Ryall, and his team have made in this ar ea. Health is one of
the few Budget portfolio areas, across all the portfolios, wher e we have actually been
able to increase funding. Constituents will be pleased to know that health alone has
received $1.5 billion worth of additional funding over a 3-year period, which is
absolutely fantastic.
The recessionary environment in which National became the Government was an
extremely difficult environment to come in to. Many people would have said that the
Government needed to cut its cloth to fit the revenue that was coming in the door. Well,
we took a very practical approach to this, and there were some key areas within the
Government spend—health being one of those and education being another of those key
areas—where we continue to spend at and beyond the level we were previously
spending. We are investing in the health of our community and in our education. There
is nothing surer. It has paid huge dividends, particularly with the six key areas of focus
that Tony Ryall has brought in with the ne w national standards in health. They are
absolutely fantastic. In terms of cancer treatm ent, the Minister has focused each of the
district health boards on lifting the bar in  terms of cancer treatment. Focusing on that
has made a huge difference.
Take immunisation. I know that in my own province of Hawke’s Bay, the Hawke’s
Bay District Health Board and its immunisa tion team have lifted the level of child
immunisation to levels that we would not ha ve anticipated 2 or 3 years ago. As a team,
through the district health nurses, they have done a fantastic job. It is interesting that the
Labour Opposition would take time to criticise district health nurses and the work that
they do in our communities to immunise young babies and to improve the health and
welfare of groups in poverty. I think that work is fantastic, but Labour is concerned
about it and that is a worry.
There have been other standards we have  focused on, such as elective surgery. We
have lifted the level of elective surgery, despite the difficult times. That has been
absolutely fantastic. We have seen accident and emergency waiting times improve
throughout district health board s around the country. Cardiovasc ular services have also
improved. A wonderful initiative from the Hawk e’s Bay District Health Board has been
a nurse-led initiative to allow prescribing of diabetes medicines, which is a wonderful
enabler that the Minister of  Health, Tony Ryall, has implemented in this term of
Government. It is absolutely fantastic. Sm oking cessation is another focus we have in
this Government, which is absolutely marvellous.
One of the things I want to focus on in the estimates debate is the more than $500
million being invested in hospital capital projects. I was particularly fortunate to be at
the Napier Health Centre on Wellesley Road  on Monday, where, as part of that $500
4 Aug 2011 Estimates Debate 20373
million capital investment, we were able to open a new digital X-ray facility. Absolutely
sensational.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: It was Labour who put that money in.

items.speaker: CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: The project started just 3 months  ago. I am not sure how that
could have been started unde r the Labour Government if it was started 3 months ago
and is being implemented now.
Let us talk about the Napier Health Cent re, which was going to close under Labour.
That is what was going to happen under Labour. It was getting to the end of its 10-year
lease, and the previous Government was going to close that centre.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: What rubbish!

items.speaker: CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: Well, if that is rubbish, then what was the protest that I was a
part of in the last term of Government? It was to make sure that that facility stayed open
for the citizens of Napier, and it has. What is more important is that we have signed a
10-year lease now—in this te rm of Government; not under a Labour Government—that
will ensure the longevity of that service fo r Napier residents. With this new digital
radiology facility, I acknowledge Wietske Cloo, Andrew Lesperance, and Warrick
Frater, who have brought about all these new services, and Mandy Robinson, who will
head up the new digital service in Hawke’s Bay. This is fantastic.
In particular, I acknowledge the board of the district health  board, led by Kevin
Atkinson. He has done an amazing job of ensuring that that district health board will be
one of the more profitable one s going forward, or that at least it will break even and
reach profitability, which will be the first time we have seen that in many, many years.
That is absolutely fantastic. Kevin has done an outstanding job.
A party vote was called for on the question, That Vote Health be agreed to.
Ayes 65
New Zealand National 57; ACT New Zealand 4; Māori Party 3; United Future 1.
Noes 53
New Zealand Labour 42; Green Party 9; Progressive 1; Independent: Carter C.
Vote Health agreed to.
Vote State Services agreed to.
Vote ACC

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: It is a great pleasure to be standing
before the Committee of the whole House for the estimates debate on Vote ACC in far
stronger circumstances. In other years in which I have been before the Committee I
have had to acknowledge huge, multibillion-do llar losses. I have had to acknowledge
that there has been—

items.speaker: Hon Steve Chadwick
items.text: Created.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The member interjects “Created.” Righty-o, she needs to
explain this point for me. ACC had a loss of $2.4 billion in 2007-08.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Oh, that’s rubbish.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The member says it is rubbi sh. Whose signature is on the
annual report showing a $2.4 billion loss? It is that of the Labour Minister of the time,
Maryan Street. So for Sue Moroney and Steve Chadwick to say that what I said is not
true is to say that Maryan St reet signed false accounts. That is what they are asserting,
and I think that is a very serious charge, for which they should perhaps go to the Serious
Fraud Office. To say that someone signed a set of accounts that was false is a very
serious accusation, which they are making agai nst Maryan Street, and I ask them to
reflect on that.
20374 Estimates Debate 4 Aug 2011
The fact is that ACC claims costs be tween 2005 and 2008 went up by 50 percent.
Claims costs were up by 50 percent. It was out  of control. It was financially reckless.
The previous Government breached the Public  Finance Act. It did not disclose the size
of the problems in the pre-election update, a nd this Government has had a hard job to
sort out that mess.
The great news for New Zealand households th is year is that we  are able to have
substantive levy reductions for households and for businesses at a time when they are
under real financial pressure. Let me tell members how much it means. It means that
workers on the average wage next year will receive a 17 percent reduction in their
earners levies, which will put 10 bucks a w eek into the hands of the average Kiwi
household. Ten bucks a week for the average Kiwi household—I thin k that is a great
thing, and I commend the work of the board and the staff of ACC.
Even better, we are able to reduce business costs. There is a 22 percent reduction in
the levies for businesses. The people who have achieved that have to be encouraged and
congratulated.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: I thought you said it was broke.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Exactly; it was, when we had reckless financial
management. Let me tell members how bad it was. When Labour was in charge, ACC
lost $4.8 billion in just 1 year.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: An investment.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The member interjects “investments”. I am happy to bet her
the best bottle of Nelson wine that of  that $4.8 billion loss—do members know how
much was lost in investments?

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: Zero?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Zero. Not one penny. That is absolutely the truth, and I
challenge the member who is interjecting to  show me, in those financial accounts from
when she was in the Government, what part of that $4.8 billion loss was in investments,
because it was not a dollar. It was not a do llar. That is in the accounts audited by the
Auditor-General.

items.speaker: Hon Steve Chadwick
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Chairperson. This is all very
interesting from the Minister, but I thought we  were in the estimates debate, which is
about this year, not the term of the previous Government.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: The member is correct, but the Minister in the
chair, the Minister for ACC, is responding to interjections. It  is rather hard to curtail
him when he has been somewhat induced to respond to a series of interjections. If
members want him to stay on track, I suggest they curtail the interjections somewhat.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Chairperson. With respect, I
think if you review the tape you will find that before any interjections occurred the
Minister opened his speech by recasting histor y, rather than dealing with the estimates,
then interjections followed after that. The Minister broke the Standing Orders
immediately he spoke, and I ask you to bring him back to the estimates.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I think that is also a fair comment, so I would
ask the Minister to address the estimates.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: These estimates provide for the ongoing huge
improvements in rehabilitation within ACC. If we are to make progress, the real key is
to make sure that we get people back to work as quickly as possible. Stunning results
are shown by programmes like Better at Wor k, which are supported in these estimates.
Although Labour feels far more comfortable w ith people sitting on welfare and people
sitting on accident compensation, we in the Government want to work on people being
able to focus on what they can do. Pr ogrammes like Better at Work, which are
4 Aug 2011 Estimates Debate 20375
supported in these estimates, are the way in  which we can rightly deliver accident
compensation in New Zealand.
There is a further very im portant change, and it is we lcomed. This year we are
introducing experience rating and a no-claims bonus for small businesses. There are
290,000 small businesses right now receiving no-claims bonuses for their improved
workplace safety. I think it is a good thing to reward workplaces that have better safety
practices and are able to avoid claims. The experience rating is an equally important
reform.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Climate Change

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: I am delighted to take th is opportunity to speak in
the estimates debate on Vote Climate Change. It is well understood that climate change
is one of the most difficult issues for Govern ments today, so it is to the enormous credit
of the Minister for Climate Change Issues, the Hon Dr Nick Smith, that New Zealand’s
modified emissions trading scheme has b een introduced so smoothly, and that in a
relatively short time it has so effectively ch anged investment patterns in our economy.
New Zealand introduced its emissions trading scheme because it is the lowest-cost way
to reduce our emissions on greenhouse gases.  As an environmentally aware country
with a “clean, green” brand, we need to be serious about reducing greenhouse gas
emissions. Putting a price on carbon is the most credible and least costly way to reduce
emissions. That is because the emissions trading scheme passes on the costs of reducing
emissions to emitters, as they are best pla ced to find the most cost-effective way of
doing this.
How well has our emissions trading scheme  done? Well, forestry entered into the
scheme in 2008, and since then there has be en a sharp switch from deforestation to
afforestation. Deforestation hit a record  of 4,000 hectares between 2005 and 2008, but
since forestry entered the scheme, new forest plantings have grown each year, with
8,000 hectares expected in 2011. This change reflects both the significant cost of
permanently removing forests and the valuable  income stream from new forests in the
emissions trading scheme.
The increase in afforestation has had a dramatic impact on New Zealand’s net
emissions, and it is essential to meeting our Kyoto obligations over the period 2008-12.
On 1 July 2010 energy, transport, and indu stry entered the scheme. Emissions from
electricity have grown 130 percent since 1990, which is the largest increase in any
sector, but the emissions trading scheme has changed th at. In 2010 the industry
achieved a 12-year high in renewable generation, of 79 percent.

items.speaker: Hon Steve Chadwick
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Chairperson. I have been listening
very carefully to the speech, but I have not heard estimates mentioned yet. We have had
a wonderful history about the emissions tr ading scheme, which Labour introduced, but
we have not heard yet about estimates. This  is a Budget debate on Vote Climate
Change.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I think the member has been talking about
current things that are in the estimates. She should perhaps make the comparative
illustration, but she has not been too far from the mark. This is a caution to all members:
this is the estimates debate.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Chairperson. Again, with
respect, as you would quite rightly concur, the estimates are forward-looking documents
as to how the Government proposes to sp end public funds. Although I am sure the
emissions trading scheme forms part of that , the member has give n us a history lesson
in respect of the emissions trading sche me and talked about industry and how many
20376 Estimates Debate 4 Aug 2011
forests have been felled and what ha ve you. The estimates are about how the
Government proposes to spend money. The member has not been around long
enough—New Zealand Bill of Rights Act aside—to work that through.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I have cautioned the member. Current policy is
relevant, but the whole speech should not dwell on that. It is really the estimates that we
are referring to.

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: I think it is particularly relevant  that the costs of afforestation
will make sure we meet the Kyoto Protocol. If  we do not meet that protocol, it will be
very expensive for our Government when we look at the 2008-12 period.
I will focus on renewable generation. I think it is important that we understand that
increased renewables will help  us in the future in mana ging our carbon footprint. The
growth of renewables has increased. I think we have already mentioned in the Chamber
that 1,340 megawatts of renewable generating capacity has been consented in the past
year, with no fossil fuel plants. That is a fi vefold increase in renewables compared with
the last decade, and that will help us manage the cost of carbon.
During the last 12 months the emissions tr ading scheme has performed well, and we
expect it to continue to do so. Actual emissions have proven to be significantly less than
those estimated, and it was expected that ove r the first reporting period the combined
industrial, electricity, and transport sectors would have emitted approximately 18.8
million tonnes, but emissions were only 16.3 million tonnes. That means that our
liability is absolutely decreased.
We can clearly see that a price on carbon ha s now been factored into New Zealand’s
economy, and that this price is helping us to achieve the Government’s goal of reducing
emissions and managing the costs of New Zealand’s international climate change
obligations.
I would like to reflect on the fact that  New Zealanders do enjoy our beautiful
country, they do appreciate its great outdoors, and they are very k een to do their bit
towards managing climate change, even if it  is costing them. I think the emissions
trading scheme is helpful in this.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I am delighted to
talk in this estimates  debate on climate change. Does  it not speak volumes about the
level of confidence there is  in the Government’s polic y around climate change that
neither the Green Party nor the Labour Party want to take a single call? I think that says
the policy is actually in really robust shape, that there is a high level of confidence about
the Government’s policies, a nd, ultimately, that they are working. Let me go through a
number of ways in which they are working, including in terms of how that will flow
through to 2011.
One of the key objectives for the Government is to reverse the awful deforestation
that occurred during the term of the previous  Government. In this year we are dealing
with, officials estimate there will be 5,700 addi tional hectares of forest. Let us compare
how that works. In the previous decade th ere was a huge increase in deforestation; the
worst period of deforestati on since records began in the 1930s was under the previous
Government. So when we introduced our po licies around climate change, we wanted to
reverse that, and we have achieved just that, with an increase in afforestation for every
single year we have been the Government, and that is continuing on into this year.
A second key objective for the Government and our climate change policies is that
we think we should be producing more of our  energy from renewables. New Zealand is
actually more privileged than most countries in that regard. What actually happened was
that during the term of the previous Gove rnm ent we saw a constant decline in the
proportion of electricity that wa s renewable. Most of the power stations that were built
4 Aug 2011 Estimates Debate 20377
under Labour were thermal fossil-fuelled power stations. In the last year we have seen a
huge improvement in that regard. It is as impressive as this: a fivefold increase—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: How many?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: —a fivefold increase—that is a 500 percent increase—in
the amount of consenting for renewables.

items.speaker: Brendon Burns
items.text: Isn’t that unbelievable?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: It is very unbelievable. Mr Burns says it is unbelievable. It
is unbelievably good, and that is what we get under a National Government. The
interesting thing is this: in terms of this fu ture year, we are expe cting to see, and the
Government is budgeting for, an ongoing improvement in the proportion of renewables,
and that is to be celebrated.
The third element is, of course—and this is absolutely pivotal to estimates—what the
cost to taxpayers will be of meeting our  Kyoto obligations. Again, let me show
members how it works. Under the Labour Government, emissions increased by 23
percent. This was the Government that cam paigned on being carbon neutral, that said
when it came to Government it would reduce emissions by 20 percent—

items.speaker: Hon Steve Chadwick
items.text: I raise a point of or der, Mr Chairperson. I again repeat that
this debate is about the estimates in the Budget. I have not heard one word about Budget
investments since this year of 2011.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I will overrule that. I think the member is
making comparisons and projecting—looking forward. I think he is in the zone.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: They are so sensitive because their record is just so ugly.
Let me tell members the advice I received when I became Minister for the Environment.
It was that if that emissions track conti nued, the cost to the New Zealand taxpayer of
meeting our Kyoto obligations—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Chairperson. I simply ask for
your clarification. In responding to my colleagues and giving your ruling to my
colleague’s question ab out relevance to estimates, you made a comment in respect of
that that I assume means the Minister wa s adhering to the Sta nding Orders by talking
about forward-looking estimates. But you us ed what we could probably call new
parliamentary language and said he was “in the zone”. I just want you to interpret that—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Please sit down. That is rather trivial. The
member has surmised correctly.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The key issue in the estimates is how much the New
Zealand taxpayer will have to pay for New Zealand to meet its Kyoto obligations. And
the answer is absolutely not a penny. Do members know why? Under the first 2 years of
the emissions trading scheme our emissi ons have stopped going up; they have gone
down. And they have gone down so well that  New Zealand will comfortably meet its
Kyoto targets, and that is absolutely good ne ws for the taxpayer. Rather than having to
write out a cheque for $485 million to countries around the world—

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The cost to New Zealand without the emissions trading
scheme would have been $485 million. But, as a consequence of having the scheme in
place, emissions are down, we are meeting our targets, and that is extra good news—
extra good news! While the M āori Party is in the House I will acknowledge that the
only way this Government has been able to get that scheme up and running, get
emissions down, get the investment in forestry, and get the investment in renewable
energy is that the M āori Party had the wisdom to back a sensible, pragmatic emissions
trading scheme that is working for New Zealand, that is working for M āori, and that is
ensuring we meet our environmental ob ligations. I simply say how proud this
Government is of the sensible progress it ha s made, and over the cour se of dealing with
20378 Estimates Debate 4 Aug 2011
the emissions trading scheme review and working forward, our objective will be to
maintain that balance of minimising costs and maximising progress on this important
issue.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Environment

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: It is my privilege to stand and speak this
afternoon on Vote Environment. I am proud to  be one of John Key’s team and proud of
the fact that he has navigated the balance so nicely around growing the economy and
protecting the environment. I thought I woul d touch on three areas in particular, and I
want to give a very local example of how exactly that balance can be achieved.
I will talk about the creation of the E nvironmental Protection Authority, under the
leadership of Minister Nick Smith; renewable energy, which again has been touched on
by the Minister under his climate change resp onsibilities; and also  the environmental
issue that affects the Taup ō electorate more than anything, and that, of course, is water
quality and our Fresh Start for Fresh Water Clean-up Fund.
Let me start with the Environmental Prot ection Authority, because the establishment
of that authority is yet another election pr omise delivered. It was something that was
talked about in the blue-green vision document, and it is great to see it being enforced
from 1 July. Clearly, in terms of the estimates, funding has been put aside for this stand-
alone authority that provides central di rection at a national level and makes
environmental protection so much easier. It  brings together the range of regulatory
functions, but, more important, it provides th e direction that has be en so lacking under
the previous Labour Government. Regional an d district councils actually have some
guidance now in terms of providing some direction.
One of the other things that the Environmen tal Protection Authority has been able to
do is the national consenting processes. This is particularly valuable with renewable
energy projects, of which there are quite a few in the Taup ō electorate. One of the
questions that came up today in  the Chamber, which Minister Smith was talking about,
was the stunning results that we are seeing in terms of rene wable energy in this country.
We are seriously on track to achieve our target of 90 percent renewable energy by 2025,
and we have had consented in 2010 the highest  level ever in terms of generation with
renewable sources. [ Interruption] Forty-two percent was geothermal. The Taup ō
electorate is the heart of geothermal energy.
Progress reported.
Report adopted.
The House adjourned at 5.55 p.m.

SPEAKER’S RULINGS 
Committee of the Whole House—Motions to Report Progress 
Mr SPEAKER : Yesterday the Committee sought  my ruling on the moving of 
motions to report progress, a motion to do just that having b een defeated by the 
Committee of the whole House on the Education (Freedom of Association) Amendment 
Bill.  
The House has a fundamental principle th at having once dealt with a matter, it 
refrains from raising it again. Standing Order 260 establishes th is principle as a rule for 
bills, amendments, or instructions proposed that are substantially the same in effect as 
ones that have already been agreed to or defeated. Clearly, where a Committee has 
defeated a motion to report progress and a nother motion to report progress is moved 
immediately thereafter, it simply raises again the matter the Committee has already 
resolved.  
20330 Speaker’s Rulings 4 Aug 2011 
However, motions that progress be re ported during the Committee stage do not 
always raise the same considerations. The rejection of such a motion in one 
circumstance does not presuppose that it may be similarly rejected in a new Committee 
on a different day, or during the consideration of a different provision of the bill.  
Therefore, a motion to report progress moved pursuant to Standing Order 177(1) 
having been defeated by the Committee, a further motion to  report progress may not be 
moved while the procedural circumstances  remain unchanged—in other words, while 
that Committee continues to consider th e same substantive question proposed by the 
Chair.

MISUSE OF DRUGS AMENDMENT BILL 
Third Reading 
Hon PETER DUNNE (Associat e Minister of Health) : I move, That the Misuse of 
Drugs Amendment Bill be now read a third time . The third reading of this bill gives me 
a great deal of pleasur e. What began as a bill with th e primary purpose of reclassifying 
pseudoephedrine and ephedrine as class B2  controlled drugs ha s become, out of 
necessity, a bill that will al so enable the Government to  more easily deal with the 
potential harms associated with new and emerging psychoactive substances like Kronic.  
The amendment that I introduced by way of Supplementary Order Paper on Tuesday 
provides a mechanism to temporarily ban subs tances where there is reason for concern 
about their use, and that will  be achieved by issuing te mporary drug class notices for 
these particular substances. In the event that such a notice is issued for a substance or a 
product, retailers will then have 7 days to remove the produc t from their shelves and it 
must not be sold after that time. The substa nce in question will then  be referred to an 
expert committee to consider it and to make recommendations for the appropriate 
ongoing level of control of that substance.  
In the case of the products currently cau sing widespread concern—that is, the 
synthetic cannabinoids and products like Kronic—I will be issuing a temporary drug 
class notice as soon as possible after this bill receives the Royal assent next week. That 
will m
ean these products must be off the shelves no more than 1 week later. In these 
circumstances my advice to current retailers is simple: return their stocks to their 
supplier right now. Do not wait for the notice to be issued, because it is ultimately the 
distributors’ responsibility and it is they who should bear the cost, not the retailer.  
At this point I would like to thank both Ministry of Health officials and the 
Parliamentary Counsel Office for their hard work developing this Supplementary Order 
Paper. I acknowledge the effort they put into getting the drafting absolutely right, but I 
must also reiterate the point I made duri ng the Committee of the whole House that the 
provisions contained in the Supplementary Order Paper ar e not the long-term solution. 
4 Aug 2011 Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill 20349 
The Law Commission’s 45 recommendations in this area remain the goal, as there can 
be no doubt of the logic that a manufacturer of  such products shou ld be required to 
demonstrate their safety before they enter the market.  
But the Law Commission’s recommendations are very high-level and it is important 
we work through the detailed policy required to  implement such a regime, to ensure we 
get the new regulatory framew ork right. I say to those wh o have been calling for the 
immediate implementation of the La w Commission’s 144 recommendations for 
updating the Misuse of Drugs Ac t that they have either fa iled genuinely to understand 
the complexities of the issues involved or  been deliberately i gnorant in advocating 
sensationalist solutions to complex issues they were incapable of  understanding. Either 
way, we are past that now. The temporary dr ug class notification process will enable us 
to better manage the influx of new substances than the current le gislation allows. The 
Government is determined to get this right. It  is not going to  be rushed into superficial 
responses that will have to be rectified later.  
Let me now discuss the major part of th is bill as it was introduced. The Prime 
Minister released the Methamphetamine Ac tion Plan in October 2009 with an aim to 
significantly reduce the use of methamphetamine and, consequently, reduce the harms it 
causes in our communities. Methamphetamine  is the only illegal stimulant drug 
commonly manufactured in our country, an d we have very hi gh rates of use by 
international standards. Methamphetamine increases the risk of cardiovascular 
problems, convulsions, and ment al health disturbances, in cluding paranoia and violent 
behaviour. The Methamphetamine Action Plan includes a comprehensive package of 
measures to control methamphetamine precu rsors, to break dr ug supply-chains, to 
improve access and routes into drug treatment, to improve support for the community to 
combat this drug, and to pr ovide stronger leadership by the Government. The harms 
posed by the diversion of pseudoephedrine to the manufacture of methamphetamine 
outweigh the need for the ongoing over-the-c ounter availability of preparations 
containing this substance.  
Although most pseudoephedrine and ephedrine used in the ma nufacture of P has 
been sourced internationally, their reclassification as class B2 controlled drugs is still an 
important part of the equation. Police continue to find domestically sourced 
pseudoephedrine at clandestine methamphetamine laboratories. The Health Committee, 
in its report, notes that the methamphetamine market is worth about $1 billion annually, 
and that at least 10 percent of this is manufactured from domestic pseudoephedrine. 
Therefore, we cannot ignore over $100 million worth of the methamphetamine market. 
We need to compliment the valuable work of the Customs Service and the police and 
strengthen our response to domestic diversion. Reclassificat ion of these substances as 
class B2 controlled drugs will also give the police and customs increased powers to 
control supply, such as being able to obtain a warrant to intercept communications.  
As members are aware, the other amendments contained within this bill are technical 
and are necessary to clarify, ti ghten, or correct current prov isions within the Act. The 
part that generated the most attention at the Health Committee—and, indeed, it has met 
with the most opposition in the House—was the part that amends the drug paraphernalia 
provisions to close two loopholes in the Act, to enable the police and customs to enforce 
the current law effectively. I have  to confess that it strikes me as strange that there is 
such strong opposition from some members,  given that in 2003 a notice was issued 
under section 22 of the Act that prohibite d the import and supply of cannabis and 
methamphetamine utensils. All the current am endm ents do is to enable this piece of 
legislation to be enforced—in other words, to actually give effect to the 2003 order.  
This bill also removes thalidomide from class A of the Misuse of Drugs Act so that it 
can be more appropriately controlled unde r the Medicines Act. Thalidomide is not 
20350 Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill 4 Aug 2011 
psychoactive nor is it used recreationally. Its place under the Misuse of Drugs Act is an 
anomaly that will be rectified with this amen dment. The bill also corrects a problematic 
overlap between the Misuse of Drugs Amendment Act 2005 and the Hazardous 
Substances and New Organisms Act 1996 by re moving the exclusion that a hazardous 
substance cannot also be a restricted substance. I touched on this briefly on Tuesday, 
and I will make the point again: we are correcting a mistake, to enable a framework in 
place since 2005, but unable to be used due to the wording in the legisla tion, to be 
available as a regulating mechanism.  
The restricted substances regime places robust controls on low-risk psychoactive 
drugs such as so-called party pills and legal highs that would otherwise be uncontrolled. 
The amendment that is proposed in this bill will remove the barrier to the use of the 
restricted substances regime. In addition, as introduced in the Supplementary Order 
Paper on Tuesday, the bill will enable restrict ed substances to also  be considered as 
herbal smoking products for the purposes of the Smoke-free Environments Act.  
Finally, this bill will strengthen our le gislation by broadeni ng our analogue 
provisions, to make sure we are prepared  for emerging designer drugs. The controlled 
drug analogue provisions preven t a large number of substan ces treated and traded as 
legal highs in other countries, such as the substance mephedrone, from being able to be 
sold legally in New Zealand. However, it is necessary that the proposed amendment to 
our current provisions is enacted, to protect  against developments that are ongoing and 
many in the chemistry of designer drugs. I am sure that all members acknowledge that 
this is an area where we face constant challenge and change.  
This bill is an important step forward. It  is with considerable pleasure that I 
commend it to the House.

the third reading of the Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill, as we have supported it 
throughout every stage of its passage through Parliament.  
We support any measure that reduces the harm caused by the abuse and misuse of 
mind-altering substances. However, although this bill will probably not make matters 
any worse, it will do very little to reduce the harm caused by the particular set of mind-

The original Act came into force in the mid-1970s. Since then, substances have

addiction to any drug—whether it be alcohol, cannabis, P, or any other substance—has

What does this bill actually do? As the Minister said, the original intention was to

ings like Kronic, Spice,

Dr PAUL HUTCHISON (National—Hunua): In supporting this  third reading of 
the Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill, everyo ne in Parliament is aware of just how

New Zealanders are probably some of the highest users of P anywhere in the world.

available at corner dairies around our countr y, and there is a real danger of normalising 
this situation for our young people. These drugs must not be normalised. Smoking them 
has significant long-term adverse health effects, and there is no doubt that their 
psychoactive effects, when mixed with alcohol, can be hugely detrimental. 
We are all aware that the Law Commission stressed the value of rehabilitation 
services, of education, of harm minimisati on, and of a public health approach, and its 
report will be visited very seriously, I am su re, by all of us. But the Law Commission 
also stressed that there were no silver bullets to this situation. It is highly complex; there 
are no simple solutions. Abuse of drugs and the callous commercial trade associated 
with them has gone on for centuries around the world, and it has become more and more 
intense in New Zealand over recent times.  
This legislation is a part of the Nati onal Government’s response to, and battle 
against, pure methamphetamine. Reclassify ing pseudoephedrine and ephedrine as class 
B drugs carries with it a very severe pe nalty, and sends very clear messages that 
methamphetamine and its precursors in this country are utterly unacceptable. The Hon 
Peter Dunne must indeed be congratulated on bringing in his two Supplementary Order 
Papers to stop the sale of s ynthetic cannabinoids. The manuf acturers cannot be trusted; 
they are conniving and ruthless and will stop at nothing to entice young New Zealanders

GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour—Wellington Central) : It would be fair to say 
that I stand in the third reading debate as a reluctant supporter of  the Misuse of Drugs 
Amendment Bill—not because I in any way want to be seen to be endorsing the 
production of methamphetamine in New Zeal and, or in any sense countenancing or 
accepting the great harm caused by P in our co mmunity. I totally accept the need for us 
as a Parliament to work together on the scou rge that is P, and to make sure that we 
minimise harm, as my colleague Iain Lees-Galloway has said, across the spectrum of 
drug abuse. Those things we take on board. 
But as we look through the provisions in this bill I am concerned. As somebody who 
was not, for the most part, on the Health Committee when the bill was being dealt with, 
I ask myself whether this is the best use of Parliament’s time when it comes to dealing 
with questions about the Misuse  of Drugs Act. I think we ne ed to make sure that when 
we are making changes like this, the change s are long-lasting, durable, and actually 
modernise law when we should modernise law.  The Minister has taken the decision to 
use a stopgap-style approach. At one le vel we can support that, and Labour is 
supporting the bill because we recognise there is a need to do something here. But, at 
another level, the fact that the Government has dragged its heels is intensely frustrating, 
as is the fact that we have a Law Commi ssion report available to us that provides the 
basis for a full rewrite of the Misuse of Dr ugs Act, yet we are not making progress on 
that. 
I will speak about three sections of the bill. The first of those is the reclassification of 
ephedrine and pseudoephedrine. Agai n, we know that the precursors to 
methamphetamine are ephedrine and pseudoephedrine. We on this side of the House 
realise the importance of being able to deal with the supply of those precursors. But, as 
my colleague Iain Lees-Galloway has said, 90 percent, probably—maybe 80 percent, or 
with a big stretch 70 percent—of that precursor product is imported in to this country. It 
is not being bought across the counters of pha rmacies. That is the truth. As somebody, I 
might say, who is unable to use the product ph enylephrine, I find myself struggling to 
find a cold remedy available to me when suffe ring from a cold, as I am today and have 
been for the last week. Pseudoephedrine pr oducts are important to people, and I 
acknowledge that they will stil l be available via prescripti on. But the question we have 
to ask ourselves when we make law like this is whether this position is the best we can 
come to. 
I know that in the select  committee the Pharmaceutical Society of New Zealand 
stated, in fact, that the altern atives to pseudoephedrine were not as effective, and that 
they leave many people needing to visit a ge neral practitioner for a prescription for 
symptomatic relief. That exposes them and others to further infection, and poses an 
unwelcome increase in workload for general practices. So the truth is that the expert 
evidence—indeed, including evidence from so me experts within this House—is that 
pseudoephedrine products tend to be those that have the mo st effective results. There 
are alternatives to moving to a prescrip tion-based approach for pseudoephedrine and 
ephedrine products, including having models trialled in some parts of the country where 
there are pharmacy systems to detect and re port inappropriate pur chase. Those models 
could be tried. So it is reluctantly that I sa y yes, we must do so mething about this. We 
do not want to stand in the way of that; ther e are elements of this bill that are good. But 
I look at this and ask whether th is is the end result. I have a feeling that when we return 
20354 Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill 4 Aug 2011 
to these matters as part of an overall review of the Misuse of Drugs  Act, we might find 
that things change. 
I will speak briefly about the Supplement ary Order Paper that  the Minister has 
brought in about the creation of these temporary class drug notices. That is obviously 
the stopgap measure that the Minister has brought in to try to do something about 
products such as Kronic and ot hers that we have had a lo t of publicity about in recent 
times. I spoke in the Committee stage of the de bate about the fact that I am concerned 
there will be loopholes in this legislation that mean that, de spite the best efforts of the 
Minister, products with slightly different chemical make-ups  will appear on the market. 
The Minister will clamp down upon them via his Gazette notice—7 days and then it is 
off the shelf—but then, lo and behold, a nother product will appear with a slightly 
different chemical make-up and the whole pr ocess will have to be repeated over and 
over again. I do not foresee that  this legislation will remove those products from the 
market, but, as Iain Lees-Galloway has sai d, it will limit them, and it will prevent them 
from being available in so many places and from being as visible as they are now. 
Therefore, some good will be done, but I beli eve that the loopholes will be such that 
there may not actually be the amount of rest riction of supply that  the Minister would 
like to see. 
Overall, though, what this highlights is th e desperate need to change the onus of 
proof about a product, a synthetic cannabinoid product, so that before it enters the 
market in New Zealand it is properly tested and assessed. It is, in my view, ridiculous 
that we have a situation where products such as these, psychoactive substances such as 
these, can enter the New Zealand market with out any kind of tes ting. The onus of proof 
must be turned on to the producers of these products so that we do not continue to 
repeat this situation. When it comes to temporary class dr ug notices, I join with my 
colleagues in supporting the fact that a stopgap measure is available, but I am concerned 
that there are loopholes, and that the possibility of stockpiling  continues to exist. As my 
colleague—again, Iain Lees-Galloway—has sai d, let us be honest about this provision. 
Let us be honest about the fact that it is not going to rid the country of synthetic 
cannabinoids. What it is going to do is limit the way in which they are sold, and perhaps 
the amount of them that is available. We  support the provision because that is a good 
thing, but it is most certainly not the end of the story. 
The other matter I will particularly address is  the question of the long-term future of 
drug law in New Zealand. I believe that it is th e responsibility of this House to consider 
today and as soon as possi ble how we can come up w ith a whole new piece of 
legislation on the question of the Misuse of  Drugs Act. As other speakers have said 
during other stages of this debate, the Misuse  of Drugs Act is from another time. It is 
from a time when different drugs were availabl e. The availability of drugs in total was 
completely different. The Law Commission recogni sed that in its repo rt, tabled in this 
House on 3 May. That report has 144 recommendations in it. It actually includes 
making the possession of drug utensils legal, which is an interesting point given what 
we are going to be doing in this bill today. Should we come to the situation where we 
decide to implement the Law Commission’s report, we may well be undoing elements 
of what we are doing today.  
But the report also calls for a more leni ent approach to social dealers and those 
caught with small amounts of illegal drugs for personal use. The Law Commission 
President, Justice Grant Hammond, said that although the law must continue to impose 
heavy penalties on those who profit from the ma nufacture and sale of illicit drugs, there 
are compelling arguments for adopting a mo re holistic focus to individual drug 
offending. To simplify that, I say that the crim inal element around drugs is in the 
supply. We need to have a harm-minimisation approach when it comes to use and 
4 Aug 2011 Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill 20355 
personal use, and we need to ensure that we address the real crime of drugs rather than 
create crimes in an unnecessary focus on some of that individual pers onal use. This is 
not just me; this is the Law Commission. I thi nk it is vitally important today, as we pass 
what everyone in this House is acknowledging as a stopgap measure, that we 
acknowledge there is a need for a fundamental  reform of drug law in New Zealand. The 
Law Commission has given us the blueprint for that; I am disappointed that the 
Government is not moving forward more quickly on it.  
On this side of the House we know that we need to take a responsible approach, and 
send a signal to the community that the pu rveyors of synthetic cannabinoids need to 
know that their products represent a risk, and that they will not enter this market without 
being watched, closely monitored, and rem oved where possible. But I call upon the 
House to ensure that we can with all speed po ssible return to this House with a bill that 
properly addresses the misuse of  drugs, and that creates a m odern law rather than this 
kind of stopgap measure. 
KEVIN HAGUE (Green): Tēnā koe e hoa. I begin by saying that the Green Party in 
many senses agrees with our Labour coll eagues—and I paraphrase somewhat here—in 
saying that the Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill contains provisions that are a daft, 
counter-productive waste of time and effort. But unlike our Labour colleagues, because 
of that we will be voting against the bill rather  than for it. If the bill had, instead, been a 
bill that enacted provisions of the Law Co mmission’s report on the misuse of drugs or 
even the recommendations from the Law Commission in respect of the matters that this 
bill covers, we would certainly be voting for it. We would much rather that this House 
debated a bill of that sort, rather than the nonsense that is before us today.  
There is no question that many drugs cau se harm, and some kind of response by 
Government is required because of that. None the less, it is also true that many New 
Zealanders make use of drugs, especially al cohol, which is probably far and away the 
most-used drug in New Zealand. It is impor tant that the Government’s response to 
drugs and drug-related harm reflects an appr opriate balance between the benefits that, 
clearly, the individuals who use those drugs perceive that they derive from them and the 
actual evidence-based harms that result from those drugs.  
The Green Party’s policy, in fact , is that a drug-free lifestyl e is the best lifestyle to 
have. But we recognise that for many people th at is not the kind of lifestyle they will 
lead. So we say that a Government’s response to drugs must be one that is consistent—
it deals with drugs in a consistent wa y, based on their harms—and derives its 
assessment of those harms from good-quality sc ientific evidence. It is also important 
that the response should be, as  both Iain Lees-Galloway and Grant Robertson have said 
in this debate tonight, a response that is focused on reducing the health-related harm, 
rather than a punitive response to o ffending. The Law Commission’s report Controlling 
and Regulating Drugs: A Review of  the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975  provides us with an 
excellent springboard, an excellent starting point, for precisely that kind of response, for 
the first time in New Zealand.  
In many ways, the bill before us represents the antithesis of that kind of response. It 
represents the very worst aspects of the way that Governments of all stripes have 
responded to drug-related issues. It is ham-fi sted; it is slow to respond to problems that 
have existed for some time. Take the issue of synthetic cannabinoids. T he Minister is 
rushing his Supplementary Order Paper into the bill so fast that the public has had no 
say at all on the new provisions, yet these products have been on retail shelves for 5 
years. So there is no need for that urgency. It is ham-fisted, but that is easily avoided.  
The three provisions to which the Green Party has expressed objection relate to 
utensils, pseudoephedrine, and synthetic ca nnabinoids. In fact, people who would be 
committing offences under these particular provisions of the bill will simply make small 
20356 Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill 4 Aug 2011 
adjustments to their behaviour and be able to carry on, with no real change. So an awful 
lot of time, energy, and effort will have gone into achieving nothing.  
This response creates harms to others, a nd Grant Robertson has just expressed some 
of those. He is a person whom Minister Dunne  encourages, when he gets a cold, to visit 
his general practitioner, sit in the waiting room, and give his co ld to other people, 
thereby increasing the amount of illness in New Zealand society. Is that the kind of 
response that we want? I do not think so. It reflects the disproportionate response to the 
actual harms related to these particular provisions.  
Lastly, and I drew attention to this in the Committee stage, it  does violence to 
parliamentary process—and I have men tioned that in relation to synthetic 
cannabinoids—and also to the principles of lawmaking. I spoke in the second reading of 
how the provisions relating to utensils represent extremely poor drafting of New 
Zealand law. I will not repeat those same arguments that I made in earlier stages of the 
debate in relation to utensils and pseudoe phedrine, and the Minister’s sweeping powers 
relating to more or less any substance at al l. The Minister talks about provisions to 
control the supply of synthetic cannabinoids, but, in fact, the provisions in this bill go 
much, much further than that. They go to any substance at all that might cause harm.  
In the debate in this House we have ta lked about psychoactiv e substances, and, 
again, the bill is not restricted to psychoactive substances, at all. When this bill is passed 
Minister Dunne will be able to ban, for 12 months, more or less any substance at all. I 
drew attention to the fact that  he would be able to ban salt . Is that truly the kind of 
outcome that this House wants? Yet it is ex actly the kind of outcome that results from 
the ad hoc and ham-fisted way that Governments have gone about drug policy-making.  
Lastly, I want to draw the attention of  the House to a comment made by the Hon 
Peter Dunne in the Committee stage. The Hon Heather Roy and I both spoke in the 
Committee stage against the provisions that he  was attempting to introduce into the bill 
in relation to these substances. The Mini ster, speaking from the chair, made the 
comment that Heather Roy and I had never en countered a drug that we did not like. I 
draw this to the attention of the House b ecause I found that comment to be not only 
extremely offensive but also reflective of exactly the kind of empty rhetoric that has 
characterised Governments’ failed responses to the harms related to drugs. It is the kind 
of empty rhetoric that has characterised the war on drugs, which has clearly been waged 
for a very long time, as Paul Hutchison reminded the House, and has failed. It is not 
only failing; it has failed.  
What we need is not the kind of rhetoric  that Peter Dunne espouses in the House. 
What we need is goodwill, good faith, a preparedness to listen to each other, and a 
preparedness to set aside preconceived ideas of how we go about so lving this problem. 
We need, instead, to make a commitment to work with each other and to think about 
constructive and novel approaches that will actu ally reflect the reality of drugs in New 
Zealand. That is exactly what the Law Commission’s report provided us with the 
opportunity to do. I cannot believe,  in the time that was availa ble to draft this bill, that 
we could not instead have translated the Law Commission’s recommendations in 
relation to utensils, pseudoephe drine, and synthetic cannabinoids into law. Then we 
would have had a bill that we would all be voting for, and that would have achieved 
some good. Thank you.

Vote Climate Change 
NICKY WAGNER (National) : I am delighted to take th is opportunity to speak in 
the estimates debate on Vote Climate Change. It is well understood that climate change 
is one of the most difficult issues for Govern ments today, so it is to the enormous credit 
of the Minister for Climate Change Issues, the Hon Dr Nick Smith, that New Zealand’s 
modified emissions trading scheme has b een introduced so smoothly, and that in a 
relatively short time it has so effectively ch anged investment patterns in our economy. 
New Zealand introduced its emissions trading scheme because it is the lowest-cost way 
to reduce our emissions on greenhouse gases.  As an environmentally aware country 
with a “clean, green” brand, we need to be serious about reducing greenhouse gas 
emissions. Putting a price on carbon is the most credible and least costly way to reduce 
emissions. That is because the emissions trading scheme passes on the costs of reducing 
emissions to emitters, as they are best pla ced to find the most cost-effective way of 
doing this. 
How well has our emissions trading scheme  done? Well, forestry entered into the 
scheme in 2008, and since then there has be en a sharp switch from deforestation to 
afforestation. Deforestation hit a record  of 4,000 hectares between 2005 and 2008, but 
since forestry entered the scheme, new forest plantings have grown each year, with 
8,000 hectares expected in 2011. This change reflects both the significant cost of 
permanently removing forests and the valuable  income stream from new forests in the 
emissions trading scheme.  
The increase in afforestation has had a dramatic impact on New Zealand’s net 
emissions, and it is essential to meeting our Kyoto obligations over the period 2008-12. 
On 1 July 2010 energy, transport, and indu stry entered the scheme. Emissions from 
electricity have grown 130 percent since 1990, which is the largest increase in any 
sector, but the emissions trading scheme has changed th at. In 2010 the industry 
achieved a 12-year high in renewable generation, of 79 percent.

LOUISE UPSTON (National—Taup ō): It is my privilege to stand and speak this 
afternoon on Vote Environment. I am proud to  be one of John Key’s team and proud of 
the fact that he has navigated the balance so nicely around growing the economy and 
protecting the environment. I thought I woul d touch on three areas in particular, and I 
want to give a very local example of how exactly that balance can be achieved.  
I will talk about the creation of the E nvironmental Protection Authority, under the 
leadership of Minister Nick Smith; renewable energy, which again has been touched on 
by the Minister under his climate change resp onsibilities; and also  the environmental 
issue that affects the Taup ō electorate more than anything, and that, of course, is water 
quality and our Fresh Start for Fresh Water Clean-up Fund.  
Let me start with the Environmental Prot ection Authority, because the establishment 
of that authority is yet another election pr omise delivered. It was something that was 
talked about in the blue-green vision document, and it is great to see it being enforced 
from 1 July. Clearly, in terms of the estimates, funding has been put aside for this stand-
alone authority that provides central di rection at a national level and makes 
environmental protection so much easier. It  brings together the range of regulatory 
functions, but, more important, it provides th e direction that has be en so lacking under 
the previous Labour Government. Regional an d district councils actually have some 
guidance now in terms of providing some direction.  
One of the other things that the Environmen tal Protection Authority has been able to 
do is the national consenting processes. This is particularly valuable with renewable 
energy projects, of which there are quite a few in the Taup ō electorate. One of the 
questions that came up today in  the Chamber, which Minister Smith was talking about, 
was the stunning results that we are seeing in terms of rene wable energy in this country. 
We are seriously on track to achieve our target of 90 percent renewable energy by 2025, 
and we have had consented in 2010 the highest  level ever in terms of generation with 
renewable sources. [ Interruption] Forty-two percent was geothermal. The Taup ō 
electorate is the heart of geothermal energy.
